title: Levi's table (Mark 2:13–17)
hook: the healthy don't need a doctor; he came for sinners
carry: the doctor is for the sick

segments.voice: Yesterday: four men dug through a clay roof to lower their paralytic friend to Jesus. Your line was friends who dig through roofs.

Some towns have one person everybody agrees is on the wrong side. Not a criminal, exactly. Just the one nobody wants at the barbecue. In Capernaum that man sat in a booth by the road, taking tolls. His name was Levi. Jesus walks past the booth and says: follow me. Just like that, Mark says, he got up and followed. Then the gossip starts. There's a dinner at Levi's house, full of his friends, the ones decent people crossed the street to avoid. And Jesus sits down with them.
screen: `A TOLL BOOTH BY THE ROAD.` → `FOLLOW ME.` → `A HOUSE FULL OF THE WRONG PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Tax collectors in Galilee gathered tolls and duties on goods moving along the roads, for Herod's government, which answered to Rome. They were widely suspected of taking extra for themselves, and neighbors could see them as working for the occupier. So when the King James Bible says Jesus sat with "publicans and sinners", publicans being the old word for tax collectors, it means people who were written off. And in that world, eating together wasn't small. A shared table said: we belong together. Some scribes of the Pharisees ask the disciples, why does he eat with these people? It's a fair question in their world. They cared deeply about holiness, and holiness has a lot to do with who you let close. Jesus overhears, and answers with a picture anyone can understand: "They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." A doctor who only visits healthy people isn't much of a doctor. Some Christians hear good news here for anyone who feels too far gone: the table is set for exactly those people. Others hear a gentle question for the ones who feel healthy: are you sure? One more detail. Matthew's gospel tells the same story and calls the tax collector Matthew. Christian tradition has long taken Levi and Matthew to be the same man, so the toll collector may be the one whose name is on a gospel.
screen: `TOLLS, AND A BAD NAME.` · `A SHARED TABLE MEANT BELONGING.` · `THE DOCTOR IS FOR THE SICK.` · `LEVI, ALSO CALLED MATTHEW.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you'd never quite sit with, a coworker from the other side of an argument, a neighbor you've made up your mind about, a relative who votes differently, and notice what happens in your chest as you picture sharing a table with them. Don't fix it; imagine the meal anyway, what you'd order, what you might ask them. If you pray, hold that person before God for a moment.
Levi's table. A tax collector's dinner, full of people nobody wanted, and Jesus in the middle of it.
Your line: the doctor is for the sick. And Jesus pulled up a chair. One hundred sixty-four days now.

howItsDone: Many churches remember Levi's dinner in shared meals open to anyone, such as community suppers and food programs, and Christians often point to this passage when welcoming people who feel unwelcome elsewhere.

chat.says: Why did people get upset that Jesus ate dinner at Levi's house?
options: His guests were people others wrote off, and a shared table said: we belong together.
Because Levi served food at that dinner that was forbidden under the law of Moses.
Because Jesus was meant to be fasting that week and ate anyway.
chat.meaning: Tax collectors and sinners were written off, and a shared table said we belong together. A doctor is for the sick.

publicans.meaning: the old word for tax collectors
